extracted.intended_audience: poets, dramatists, and students of dramatic composition (playwrights and scholars of tragedy)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and evaluating tragic drama: plotting (recognition, reversal, complication/unravelling), diction/thought, stagecraft (scene-visualization, gestures, chorus), and language/metre/figurative language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition (Anagnorisis): modes and quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguishes kinds of recognition (tokens, poet-invented, memory, reasoning) and judges their artistic merit. 'The use of tokens for the express purpose of proof ... is a less artistic mode of recognition. A better kind is that which comes about by a turn of incident.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preferred: recognition arising 'from the incidents themselves' (natural and startling), which 'dispense with the artificial aid of tokens or necklaces.' Less artistic: formal proof by tokens or recognitions 'invented at will by the poet' (wanting in art). Other legitimate kinds: memory (sight of an object awakens feeling), and recognition by process of reasoning (logical inference). Examples and anti-patterns: Bath Scene in the Odyssey (good); Orestes who 'speaks himself' to reveal identity (bad — poet speaks rather than plot demanding it); 'voice of the shuttle' in Sophocles as another poorer device. Use recognitions that are in-keeping with plot necessity; avoid contrived disclosures where the poet makes a character speak facts the plot does not require.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visualize the scene (stage situational awareness)
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should 'place the scene, as far as possible, before his eyes' so that the action is seen vividly as by a spectator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Working with vivid visualization helps discover what is in keeping with the situation and prevents inconsistencies. Example: an oversight in Carcinus (Amphiaraus on his way from the temple) that offended the audience because the poet failed to see the situation. Rule: imagine the staging and viewpoint to avoid stage impossibilities or contradictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate gestures and physical expression
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should 'work out his play ... with appropriate gestures' because those who feel emotion are most convincing by force of sympathy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate gestural and physical action consistent with the emotion of characters: agitation manifests as storming, anger as raging, etc. This increases believability; consider naturalistic physicality in performance when composing. Note: Sympathy and conviction are heightened when physical behavior matches emotional state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outline first, then fill episodes; ensure episodes are relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: Compose by first sketching the general outline of the story, then fill in and amplify episodes, making sure episodes are relevant to the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Iphigenia — sketch the main plan (sacrifice, disappearance, transportation, danger, recognition) then fill episodes that are relevant (e.g., Orestes' madness and purificatory rite). In drama episodes should be short and directly related to the action; avoid extraneous incidents. Episodes provide extension (as in epic) but must remain subordinate to the dramatic unity of the piece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot structure: Complication and Unravelling (Dénouement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every tragedy falls into two parts — Complication (everything up to the turning-point) and Unravelling (from the beginning of the change to the end).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define which incidents form the Complication (presupposed incidents and the lead-up to reversal) and which form the Unravelling (the consequences and resolution). Example: In the Lynceus of Theodectes the Complication consists of the incidents presupposed in the drama and the seizure of the child; the Unravelling extends from the accusation of murder to the end. Use this division to shape pacing and causal logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinds of tragedy and desired combination of merits
rubrics_metrics.description: Classifies tragedies as Simple or Complex (depending on reversal and recognition), Pathetic (motive is passion), Ethical (motive ethical), and excludes supernatural kinds for ordinary tragic aims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The poet should, if possible, combine all poetic merits or at least attain the greatest number and those most important. Critics expect a single poet to excel across several lines; aim for a dominant form but incorporate other strengths where feasible. Be aware of genre expectations (e.g., avoid supernatural modes if aiming for natural tragic effect).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of plot; avoid Epic multiplicity of plots
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not structure a tragedy like an epic with multiplicity of plots; tragedy should select a portion, not dramatize an entire long narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid dramatizing the entire Iliad or the whole tale of Niobe — such multiplicity leads to failure or poor stage success. Select a coherent portion and keep the plot united (Complication + Unravelling). Example anti-patterns: poets who dramatized the whole Fall of Troy or the whole tale of Niobe failed or had poor success on stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversal (Peripeteia) and producing tragic effect; probability
rubrics_metrics.description: Reversal of the action is a central device to achieve tragic effect; such reversals should be skilfully arranged and compatible with probability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A successful reversal produces a tragic effect that satisfies the moral sense (audience’s sense of justice or irony), e.g., the clever rogue outwitted, or the brave villain defeated. Reversals should be probable or at least believable in context (Aristotle notes debate about 'probable' being used broadly). Skill in arranging reversals is a mark of the good poet; avoid implausible twists that violate audience expectations of probability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chorus integration: chorus as an actor
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chorus should be regarded as one of the actors and be an integral part of the whole, sharing in the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer Sophoclean integration in which the Chorus participates in the subject and action; avoid choral songs that are mere interludes unrelated to the piece (a later practice begun by Agathon). Treat the Chorus as contributing materially to plot, emotion, and thematic development rather than as detachable entertainment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought (Dianoia): speech effects — proof, refutation, and emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Under 'Thought' are all effects produced by speech: proof and refutation, excitation of feelings (pity, fear, anger), and the suggestion of importance or its opposite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dramatic incidents should be treated from the same points of view as dramatic speeches when aiming to evoke pity, fear, or importance: incidents should 'speak for themselves' without verbal exposition; speeches should produce the intended effects (e.g., proof or refutation). Use rhetorical devices as required (arguments, emotional arousal), but avoid redundant speech where the incident itself conveys the effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction and modes of expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction includes Modes of Expression (command, prayer, narrative, threat, question, answer, etc.), a domain related to the art of Declamation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know which verbal mode a passage requires (command vs. prayer vs. narrative, etc.). This knowledge belongs to declamation specialists, but the poet must choose appropriate verbal modes for each dramatic moment. Misclassifying modes is not a grave fault of the poet’s art but correct mode selection aids clarity and effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language elements and phonetic/metrical considerations (letters, syllables, connecting words)
rubrics_metrics.description: Language in detail: the Letter (vowel, semi-vowel, mute), the Syllable (composition and metrical relevance), and Connecting words (non-significant sounds that join significant sounds).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be conscious of phonetics and syllabic composition (vowels, semi-vowels like S and R, mutes like G and D) and how these affect audibility and metre. Syllable-formation and length, aspiration, acute/grave tones, and placement of connecting words relate to metrical effect. These finer points often belong to a treatise on metre but are relevant to diction and delivery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word choice, types, and metaphor
rubrics_metrics.description: Words may be simple, double, compound; and classified as current, strange, metaphorical, ornamental, newly-coined, lengthened, contracted, or altered. Metaphor is central: from genus to species, species to genus, species to species, or by analogy/proportion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose words with awareness of their register (current vs. strange) and function (ornamental vs. necessary). Use metaphor by transference (genus↔species, species↔species) or by proportion (analogy); qualify metaphors when needed (e.g., 'the cup is the shield of Dionysus'). Examples: 'old age is the evening of life'; 'sowing the god-created light' (sun scattering rays as sowing). Metaphor can condense complex relations and enrich diction; misuse (obscure or forced metaphors) harms clarity.
